chapters.title: Dawn of Indo - Roman Maritime Trade
Arikamedu & Muziris: Gateway to south east Asia

blocks.text: See these dots. Each one marks a Roman gold coin found buried across Europe. But look toward the east and you will notice something odd. A dense cluster of Roman gold. Far more than anywhere else, lies in India. How did a land thousands of miles away become home to a treasure trove of Roman gold? Long before the Suez Canal. India. Trade with the Arabian Peninsula was central to the Maritime Silk Road. On land, routes extended from Bactria into the northeastern part

at sea, the port of Bury Ni-ki was a prime hub connecting Indian traders to the Mediterranean world, a journey that took a full year traversing the coasts of various kingdoms. The vast open ocean was a mystery as there was no sophisticated method to navigate it accurately. But in the first century BCE, a storm washed an Indian sailor ashore in Egypt, barely clinging to life. He was brought before the Alexandrian court that the king spared his life in exchange for a secret.

A secret that gave Indian sailors the power to travel through the open sea fearlessly without ever losing the elite. The monsoon. Every July, the monsoon winds blew from west to east. Indian sailors had mastered their rhythm, harnessing them to cut a six month voyage down to just three weeks. It was a rout most sailors feared, cutting straight through the middle of the ocean. The rescued sailors later guided the king's navigator along this invisible wind road landing on India's western coast

in September, just as a rains withdrew. This open sea route wasn't just last year, it was a bypass. Persian and Arabian boats dodging taxes and middlemen. Armed with this newfound knowledge, the ships set sail again in December, returning to Egypt with Indian treasures. Now, before I continue, there is no direct record of who reveal the secret of our key source. The very place makes no mention. However, the story appears in other sources, and New Scientist Sheila DePatie

has stated that the people of Indus Valley Civilization were already using monsoon winds for maritime trade as early as 2500 BC, and even published research to prove it. Link in the description. Back to the story. In 30 B.C., the Red sea welcomed a new ruler, Augustus. The Roman Empire had expanded, taking control of Egypt and the Mediterranean. This was the dawn of indoor Roman trade. Over 120 ships departed annually from Musa Hormuz, ferrying gold

in exchange for spices, gems and silk during this flourishing Indo Roman trade. An event took place which left the entire Roman world stunned. An Indian king sent an embassy, though we still don't know which king. That's not the point. What matters is that this embassy shocked the Roman world for centuries. Alongside diplomats letters and a live tiger game of Śramaṇa a monk devoted to peace through personal suffering in the heart of Athens, this monk self immolated before the crowd. The story spread like wildfire.

He was buried in Athens with a local name, Zarmanochegas on his tomb. It was inscribed that he came from a place called Barygaza an ancient port named after the sage Bhrigu, which Indians called Bharuch. It was no ordinary port. It played a pivotal role in the street network. Gifted with geographical advantage, Bharuch was situated on the banks of the river, serving as an entrance to the inland territories. The monsoon winds we talked about felt they drove ships directly towards shore. The Western Kshatrapas

recognized these advantages and made Bharuch the maritime gateway. It was also around this time that Hippalus credited by the Greeks with discovering the monsoon routes, helped Bharuch cement its position as India's golden door to Rome. As Baruch flourished, so did other. Muziris in Kerala. Known as the first Emporium of India became a magnet for global trade. Christians believed that Saint Thomas, one of Jesus 12 apostles, arrived here to spread the gospel and betted in India that he still venerated today.

But his arrival came Jewish settlers, many of whom returned to Israel after World War Two. That story deserves its own deep dive, so we'll cover it sometime later. Arikamedu, near modern-day Pondicherry connected Roman traders with Southeast Asian nations, strengthening ties and expanding the trade network for the East. As these new port thrived, the Indo Roman trade grew immensely, worth over 100 million censuses annually and Roman gold. Pliny the Elder, the famous Roman author and commander, complained that Roman gold

was draining into India to feed the luxurious desires of Roman society. This was the era when Roman gold flooded India. During his reign, the empire even minted coins featuring Greek and Roman deities. Indian deities made their way to Greece and Rome, appearing in palace decor. Tamil literature also mentions Romans serving as bodyguards for Tamil kings. Trade and prosperity were at their peak, but what goes up must come down. Decline began with political instability and baroque

The Kshatrapas fell, and Bharuch lost its guardians. Then the Guptas fell too, and Bharuch strategic value diminished as different rulers had different priorities. Meanwhile, Rome faced its own chaos. The assassination of Alexander Severus led to the eventual split of the empire. A financial crisis followed and gold grew scarce. New Roman coins minted with base metals were rejected by most Indian traders. Trade slowed, luxuries became unaffordable. It didn't vanish entirely. Textiles continued to be traded.

There is even evidence of trade between Indians and Emperor Justinian one, but it never returned to its former glory. Eventually, Persian rulers dominated the trade routes, growing richer and more powerful. The Western Roman Empire collapsed altogether when Odoacer overthrew the last Roman emperor. The final chapter came in the seventh century. The rise of Islamic empires swept across Arabia and North Africa, taking over the regions that once connected India to Rome. Indo Roman trade came to an end, replaced by new Islamic networks
using the old routes the ports once lived with Rome and gold now lie buried in silence. What remains are ruins and millions of Roman gold coins found far from the empire that minted them.
